lesson.title: One Row at a Time: Understanding Observations
lesson.summary: This section defines an observation as the complete set of recorded values for a single individual, and distinguishes it from a variable, which is a single characteristic measured across many individuals.
lesson.body:
Data, as defined earlier, is the full collection of recorded facts a researcher gathers. A variable, as defined in the previous section, is a single characteristic that is measured, like quiz score or height. An observation is the third piece of this puzzle: it is the complete set of recorded values belonging to one single individual, whether that individual is a person, a store, a day, or a country. If a variable is a column of information, an observation is a row.

Return once more to the classroom example. The teacher recorded quiz score and height for 8 students. One student, the first one in the list, has a quiz score of 7 and a height of 61 inches. Together, that pair of numbers, 7 and 61, is her observation: everything the teacher recorded about that one specific student. Another student has a quiz score of 8 and a height of 64 inches, forming a different observation. There are 8 students, so there are 8 observations in this dataset, one for each student, even though there are only 2 variables being tracked.

It is easy to confuse an observation with a variable, especially early on, so it is worth stating the difference plainly one more time. A variable answers the question "what was measured." An observation answers the question "who or what was it measured on, and what were all their values." When you read a row across a table, you are reading an observation. When you read a column down a table, you are reading a variable. Every cell in the table, meanwhile, is a single value: one variable's recorded value for one observation.

Here is a worked example that shows why keeping observations intact matters. Suppose we want to know whether taller students in the class tend to score higher on the quiz. To answer that, we cannot just look at the list of quiz scores by itself, and separately look at the list of heights by itself. We need to look at them together, observation by observation, so we know that the student who is 66 inches tall is the same student who scored a 9, and not some other student. If the teacher recorded a quiz score of 9 for the student who is 66 inches tall, and a quiz score of 5 for the student who is 59 inches tall, comparing those two paired observations, height 66 with score 9 versus height 59 with score 5, gives real information about whether the two variables tend to move together. Scrambling which score belongs to which height would destroy that information completely, even though the underlying lists of numbers looked exactly the same.

Understanding observations as complete, connected units is what allows all of the recorded information about the 8 students to be organized into a single structured table. That table, where every row is one observation and every column is one variable, is exactly what the next section calls a dataset.
